nodes.statement: Our thesis follows at once from Lemma \ref{lemmacomorphismsofsitesgenerators} in light of the fact that, as recalled above, the Grothendieck topology $M^{F}_{L}$ is generated by the pullback-stable collection of sieves of the form $\{f:{\rm dom}(f)\to c \mid F(f)\in R\}$ where $R$ varies among the $L$-covering sieves on $F(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3.5 to the generators of $M^F_L$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Full faithfulness gives cover-reflection
nodes.statement: Let us now suppose that $F$ is full and faithful. If $S$ is a sieve such that $F(S)$ is $K$-covering then the family $\{g\in {\cal C} \mid F(g)\in \langle F(S)\rangle \}$ is $M^{F}_{K}$-covering. But, since $F$ is full and faithful, $F(g)\in \langle F(S)\rangle $ if and only if $g\in \langle S\rangle $, so $S$ is $M^{F}_{K}$-covering, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Full faithfulness gives cover-reflection
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: $C_i$ is an inclusion, so $(C_i)_!$ reflects isomorphisms
nodes.statement: We preliminarily observe that, since $i$ is $K$-full and $K$-faithful, $C_{i}$ is an inclusion by Proposition \ref{propinclusioncomoprhismofsites}, equivalently the functor $(C_{i})_{!}$ is full and faithful. So $(C_{i})_{!}$ reflects isomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: $C_i$ is an inclusion, so $(C_i)_!$ reflects isomorphisms
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Continuity gives the commutative square
nodes.statement: Since $i$ is $(K, J)$-continuous, by Corollary \ref{corequivcharcanonicity} we have a commutative square \[ \xymatrix{ [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{\textup{Lan}_{i^{\textup{op}}}} \ar[d]^{a_{K}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[d]^{a_{J}} \\ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K) \ar[r]^{(C_{i})_{!}} & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) } \]
nodes.statement_short: Continuity gives the commutative square
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Read off the characterization of $K$
nodes.statement: Now, the commutativity of this diagram implies that the canonical morphism $m_{T}:T\rightarrowtail y_{\cal D}(d)$ is sent by $(C_{i})_{!} \circ a_{K}$ to an isomorphism (equivalently, since $(C_{i})_{!}$ reflects isomorphisms, $T$ is $K$-covering) if and only $a_{J}$ sends $\textup{Lan}_{i^{\textup{op}}}(m_{T})$ to an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Read off the characterization of $K$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: $i$ is a comorphism into $({\cal C},J\vee R_i)$
nodes.statement: As observed above, $i$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J})\to ({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i})$.
nodes.statement_short: $i$ is a comorphism into $({\cal C},J\vee R_i)$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: $i$ is continuous, so Proposition 3.8 applies
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by our hypothesis, $i$ is also a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J})\to ({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i})$ and hence it is $(K, J\vee R_{i})$-continuous. We can therefore apply Proposition \ref{proprecoverytopologycontinuity} to it.
nodes.statement_short: $i$ is continuous, so Proposition 3.8 applies
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Bicovering of ${\rm Lan}(m_T)$ amounts to $i(T)$ covering
nodes.statement: But, since $a_{J\vee R_{i}}\circ \textup{Lan}_{i^{\textup{op}}}$ preserves finite limits and hence monomorphisms, $\textup{Lan}_{i^{\textup{op}}}(m_{T})$ is $(J\vee R_{i})$-bicovering if and only if the flat functor $a_{J}\circ \textup{Lan}_{i^{\textup{op}}}\circ y_{\cal D}=l_{\cal C}\circ i$ sends $T$ to an epimorphic family of ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i})$, that is, if and only if $i$ sends $T$ to a $(J\vee R_{i})$-covering family.
nodes.statement_short: Bicovering of ${\rm Lan}(m_T)$ amounts to $i(T)$ covering
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Correspondence of subtoposes via the inclusion $C_i$
nodes.statement: Consider the geometric morphism $C_{i}:[{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]\to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ induced by $i$; it is an inclusion (cf. Remark \ref{remarkinclusion}) and hence we have a bijective correspondence between the subtoposes of $[{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ (equivalently, the Grothendieck topologies on $\cal D$) and the subtoposes of $[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ which are contained in $C_{i}$ (equivalently, the Grothendieck topologies $J$ on $\cal C$ which contain the rigid topology $R_{i}$ whose covering sieves on an object $c$ are the sieves containing all the arrows from objects of the form $i(d)$ to $c$). Given a Grothendieck topology $K$ on $\cal D$, the Grothendieck topology on $\cal C$ associated with it via this correspondence is precisely the topology $K^{i}$ coinduced by $K$ along $i$ (in the sense of Proposition \ref{propimagetopology}). On the other hand, for any Grothendieck topology $J$ on $\cal C$, the Grothendieck topology on $\cal D$ associated with the intersection of the subtoposes ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ and $C_{i}$ (that is, with the Grothendieck topology on $\cal C$ generated by $R_{i}$ and $J$) is the smallest Grothendieck topology $M^{i}_{J}$ on $\cal D$ which makes $i$ a comorphism of sites to $({\cal C}, J)$. Indeed, $M^{i}_{J}$ is characterized in the proof of Lemma C2.3.19 \cite{El} by the pullback square \[ \xymatrix{ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \ar[d] \\ [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{C_{i}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }], } \] from which it is clear that subtopos given by the composite of ${\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J})\hookrightarrow [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ with $C_{i}$ is precisely the subtopos of $[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ given by the intersection of the subtoposes ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ and $C_{i}$. This shows that $J\vee R_{i}=(M^{i}_{J})^{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Correspondence of subtoposes via the inclusion $C_i$; derive $J\vee R_i=(M^i_J)^i$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: $i$ is a comorphism $({\cal D},M^i_J)\to({\cal C},J\vee R_i)$
nodes.statement: Notice that, since the equivalence $${\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J})\simeq {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i})$$ makes the square \[ \xymatrix{ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i}) \ar[d] \\ [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{C_{i}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }], } \] commute (the morphism ${\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J})\to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ is the composite of the equivalence ${\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J})\simeq {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i})$ with the canonical inclusion ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i})\hookrightarrow {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$), the functor $i$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, M^{i}_{J})\to ({\cal C}, J\vee R_{i})$ (cf. section \ref{sec:comorphismsofsites1}).
nodes.statement_short: $i$ is a comorphism $({\cal D},M^i_J)\to({\cal C},J\vee R_i)$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: The square for $K^i$ is a pullback, so $K=M^i_{K^i}$
nodes.statement: In the converse direction, for any Grothendieck topology $K$ on $\cal D$, we have a commutative square \[ \xymatrix{ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K) \ar[r] \ar[d] & {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, K^{i}) \ar[d] \\ [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{C_{i}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }], } \] where the upper horizontal morphism is an equivalence (by the universal property of the topology $K^{i}$). This square is thus a pullback and hence from the pullback characterization of the topology $M^{i}_{K^{i}}$ it follows that $K=M^{i}_{K^{i}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The square for $K^i$ is a pullback, so $K=M^i_{K^i}$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2.21 in two cases
nodes.statement: Let us now apply Proposition \ref{procofinality} in two notable cases: \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 2.21 in two cases

nodes.name: Case $F'=1_{\cal C}$: criterion for colimits to be terminal
nodes.statement: \item $F=\xi:{\cal A}\to {\cal C}$, $F'=1_{\cal C}$, $\alpha$ is the identity. In this case the equivalence relations $R'_{c}$ are the total relations, and the proposition yields the following criterion: the canonical arrow \[ \textup{colim}_{[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]}(y_{\cal C}\circ \xi) \to \textup{colim}_{[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]}(y_{\cal C})=1_{[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]} \] is sent by $a_{J}$ to an isomorphism \[ \textup{colim}_{{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)}(l\circ \xi) \to 1_{{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)} \] if and only if the following conditions are satisfied: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item For any object $c$ of $\cal C$ there are a $J$-covering family $\{f_i: c_i \to c \mid i\in I\}$ and for each $i\in I$ an object $a_{i}$ of $\cal A$ and an arrow $y_i:c_{i}\to F(a_{i})$. \item For any object $c$ of $\cal C$ and any arrows $x:c\to F(a)$ and $x':c\to F(b)$ in $\cal C$, there is a $J$-covering family $\{f_i: c_i \to c \mid i\in I\}$ such that $(x\circ f_i, x'\circ f_i)\in R_{c_{i}}$ for each $i\in I$. \end{enumerate} Notice that if $J$ is the trivial Grothendieck topology then the above conditions amount precisely to the requirement that for every object $c$ of $\cal C$, the category $(c\downarrow \xi)$ be non-empty and connected, which means precisely that the functor $F$ is cofinal (in the classical sense). It is therefore natural to call \emph{$J$-cofinal} a functor $F:{\cal A}\to {\cal C}$ which satisfies the two conditions above (see Definition \ref{defrelcofinality} below).
nodes.statement_short: Case $F'=1_{\cal C}$: criterion for colimits to be terminal; motivates $J$-cofinality

nodes.name: Case of a slice: criterion for a cocone to become a colimit
nodes.statement: \item $F'$ is the forgetful functor $U_{c_{0}}:{\cal C}\slash c_{0}\to {\cal C}$ for an object $c_{0}$ of $\cal C$, $\xi$ is a cocone $\{\xi_{a}: F(a)\to c_{0} \mid a\in {\cal A}\}$ under the functor $F$ with vertex $c_{0}$ and $\alpha$ is the identity. In this case we have: for any $y:c \to (U_{c_{0}}([p:c'\to c_{0}]))$ and $y':c \to (U_{c_{0}}([q:c''\to c_{0}]))$, $(y, y')\in R'_{c}$ if and only if $p\circ y=q\circ y'$. So the proposition yields the following criterion: the cocone $\xi$ is sent by the canonical functor ${\cal C}\to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ to a colimit if and only if the following conditions are satisfied: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item For any object $c$ of $\cal C$ and any arrow $y:c\to c_{0}$ in $\cal C$ there are a $J$-covering family $\{f_i: c_i \to c \mid i\in I\}$ and for each $i\in I$ an object $a_{i}$ of $\cal A$ and an arrow $y_i:c_{i}\to F(a_{i})$ such that $y\circ f_{i}=\xi_{a_{i}}\circ y_{i}$. \item For any object $c$ of $\cal C$ and any arrows $x:c\to F(a)$ and $x':c\to F(b)$ in $\cal C$ such that $\xi_{a}\circ x= \xi_{b}\circ x'$ there is a $J$-covering family $\{f_i: c_i \to c \mid i\in I\}$ such that $(x\circ f_i, x'\circ f_i)\in R_{c_{i}}$ for each $i\in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Case of a slice: criterion for a cocone to become a colimit

nodes.name: Introduce $W_J$, which contains $J$ and $R_i$ and is contained in $J\vee R_i$
nodes.statement: Let $W_{J}$ be the collection of sieves on $\cal C$ defined as follows: for any sieve $T$ on an object $c$ of $\cal C$, $T\in W_{J}(c)$ if and only if for every arrow $\xi:i(d)\to c$, $\xi^{\ast}(T)\in J(i(d))$. Then $J\subseteq W_{J}$ and $R_{i}\subseteq W_{J}$. Also, $W_{J}\subseteq J\vee R_{i}$ by the transitivity axiom for Grothendieck topologies.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $W_J$, which contains $J$ and $R_i$ and is contained in $J\vee R_i$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Reduce to closure of $W_J$ under multicomposition
nodes.statement: So, to show that $W_{J}=J\vee R_{i}$, it remains to verify that, under our assumption, $W_{J}$ is a Grothendieck topology. The fact that the maximality and pullback stability axioms are satisfied is clear, as it is the fact that any sieve containing a sieve in $W_{J}$ lies again in $W_{J}$. So it remains to show that arbitrary multicompositions of sieves in $W_{J}$ lie in $W_{J}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to closure of $W_J$ under multicomposition
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Verify closure under multicomposition using the hypothesis on ${\rm Im}(i)$
nodes.statement: So, suppose that $S\in W_{J}(c)$ and that, for each $f\in S$, $S_{f}\in W_{J}({\rm dom}(f))$. Then the sieve $S\ast \{S_{f} \mid f\in S\}$ belongs to $W_{J}(c)$ since for any $\xi:i(d)\to c$, $\xi^{\ast}(S\ast \{S_{f} \mid f\in S\})$ contains the multicomposition $(\xi^{\ast}(S)\cap \textup{Im}(i)) \ast \{S_{\xi\circ g} \mid g\in (\xi^{\ast}(S)\cap \textup{Im}(i))\}$, all of whose sieves are $J$-covering (note that $S_{f}$ is $J$-covering for any arrow $f$ whose domain is of the form $i(d)$ for an object $d\in {\cal D}$).
nodes.statement_short: Verify closure under multicomposition using the hypothesis on ${\rm Im}(i)$
nodes.section: 3.3.1 The smallest Grothendieck topology making a functor a comorphism of sites

nodes.name: Prove (i) by lifting $\beta$ up to isomorphism
nodes.statement: (i) The inclusion $\subseteq$ is obvious (and holds in general), so we have to show the converse one. Given $r\in \langle p(P)\rangle $, $r=p(f)\circ \beta$ for some $f\in P$ and arrow $\beta$ in $\cal D$. Since $p$ is a fibration, there is an isomorphism $\alpha$ such that $\beta\circ \alpha=p(g)$ for some arrow $g$ to ${\rm dom}(f)$ in $\cal C$. So $r\circ \alpha=p(f)\circ \beta\circ \alpha=p(f)\circ p(g)=p(f\circ g)$; in other words, $r=p(f\circ g)\circ \alpha^{-1}$. Since $f\circ g\in \langle P\rangle $, $r\in \overline{p(\langle P\rangle )}^{i}$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (i) by lifting $\beta$ up to isomorphism

nodes.name: Prove (ii) via a cartesian lift of $r$
nodes.statement: (ii) The inclusion $\subseteq$ is obvious (and valid in general), so we only have to prove the converse one. Given $f\in S^{p}_{\langle R\rangle }$, $p(f)\in \langle R\rangle $, i.e. $p(f)=r\circ \gamma$ for some $r\in R$. Since $f$ is a fibration, there is a cartesian arrow $\phi$ and an isomorphism $\delta$ such that $r\circ \delta=p(\phi)$. Now, since $\phi$ is cartesian and $p(f)=p(\phi)\circ (\delta^{-1} \circ \gamma)$, there exists a unique arrow $\psi$ such that $p(\psi)=\delta^{-1} \circ \gamma$ and $f=\phi\circ \psi$. Now, since $p(\phi)=r\circ \delta$, $\phi\in S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}}$, whence $f\in \langle S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}}\rangle $.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (ii) via a cartesian lift of $r$

nodes.name: Prove (iii) via the vertical-cartesian factorization
nodes.statement: (iii) Let us first prove that $S^{p}_{\overline{p(P)}^{i}}\supseteq \overline{P^{\textup{cart}}}^{v}$. Let us consider ` the' factorization $\phi_{u}\circ \gamma$ of $u$ as a vertical arrow followed by a cartesian arrow. Given $f\in \overline{P^{\textup{cart}}}^{v}$, there is an arrow $u\in P$ and a vertical arrow $s$ such that $f=\phi_{u}\circ s$, where $\phi_{u}$ is ` the' cartesian image of $u$. Then $p(f)=p(\phi_{u})\circ p(s)$ and, since $p(s)$ is an isomorphism, $p(f)=p(u)\circ p(\gamma)^{-1}\circ p(s)\in \overline{p(P)}^{i}$, as required. Conversely, let us suppose that $f\in S^{p}_{\overline{p(P)}^{i}}$. Then $p(f)=p(u)\circ \alpha$ for some arrow $u\in P$ and some isomorphism $\alpha$. Since $\phi_{u}$ is cartesian, there is an arrow $\psi$ such that $p(\psi)=p(\gamma)\circ \alpha$ and $f=\phi_{u}\circ \psi$. So $\psi$ is a vertical arrow and hence $f\in \overline{P^{\textup{cart}}}^{v}$, as required. The second statement follows from the first in light of (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Prove (iii) via the vertical-cartesian factorization

nodes.name: Prove (iv) by double inclusion
nodes.statement: (iv) Let us start showing that $\overline{R}^{i}\subseteq \overline{p(S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}})}^{i}$, equivalently, that $R\subseteq \overline{p(S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}})}^{i}$. Given $r\in R$, since $p$ is a fibration, there is a cartesian arrow $\phi$ to $c$ and an isomorphism $\alpha$ such that $r=p(\phi)\circ \alpha$. Therefore $\phi\in S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}}$ and hence $r\in \overline{p(S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}})}^{i}$. Conversely, suppose that $u\in \overline{p(S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}})}^{i}$. Then $u=p(f)\circ \delta$ for some arrow $f\in S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}}$ and isomorphism $\delta$. Now, since $f\in S^{p}_{\overline{R}^{i}}$, $p(f)=r\circ \beta$ for some arrow $r\in R$ and isomorphism $\beta$. So $u=r\circ (\alpha\circ \beta)$ and hence $u\in \overline{R}^{i}$. The second statement clearly follows from the first, since taking the sieve generated by a presieve $S$ is the same as taking the sieve generated by the presieve $\overline{S}^{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (iv) by double inclusion

nodes.name: Prove (v): $S^p_R$ is closed under vertical precomposition
nodes.statement: (v) This follows from the fact that $S^{p}_{R}$ satisfies the property that for any vertical arrow $v$ and any arrow $b$ composable with it $b\circ v\in S^{p}_{R}$ if and only if $b\in S^{p}_{R}$ (since $p(v)$ is an isomorphism and $R$ is a sieve).
nodes.statement_short: Prove (v): $S^p_R$ is closed under vertical precomposition

nodes.name: Prove (vi) by double inclusion using (iv) and cartesianness
nodes.statement: (vi) Let us set $R:=p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P)\rangle )$. By (iv), we have $R=\langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle $, so it is equivalent to prove that $\langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle =\langle p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\rangle $. Let us first show that $\langle p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\rangle \subseteq \langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle $, or equivalently that $p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\subseteq \langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle $. This inclusion does not exploit the hypothesis that $P$ only consist of cartesian arrows. Given $s\in p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))$, $s=p(g)$ where $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$. Now, $g\in S^{p}_{R}$. Indeed, $p(g)\in R=p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P)\rangle )$ as $p(f)\circ p(g)=p(f\circ g)\in p(\langle P\rangle )\subseteq \langle p(P)\rangle $. So $g=p(s)\in p(S^{p}_{R})$, as required. Conversely, let us show that $p(S^{p}_{R})\subseteq \langle p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\rangle $. Given $s\in p(S^{p}_{R})$, we have an arrow $g\in S^{p}_{R}$ such that $s=p(g)$. Let us show that $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$. Since $p(g)\in R=p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P)\rangle )$, $p(f)\circ p(g)=\xi\circ \gamma$ for some arrow $\xi\in P$ and some arrow $\gamma$. Now, since $\xi$ is cartesian (by our hypothesis every arrow of $P$ is cartesian), there is a unique arrow $\psi$ in $\cal C$ such that $p(\psi)=\gamma$ and $\xi\circ \psi=f\circ g$. So $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (vi) by double inclusion using (iv) and cartesianness

nodes.name: Reduce via (iv) to an equality of generated sieves
nodes.statement: (vi) Let us set $R:=p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P)\rangle )$. By (iv), we have $R=\langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle $, so it is equivalent to prove that $\langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle =\langle p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\rangle $.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via (iv) to an equality of generated sieves

nodes.name: First inclusion, not using cartesianness
nodes.statement: Let us first show that $\langle p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\rangle \subseteq \langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle $, or equivalently that $p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\subseteq \langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle $. This inclusion does not exploit the hypothesis that $P$ only consist of cartesian arrows. Given $s\in p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))$, $s=p(g)$ where $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$. Now, $g\in S^{p}_{R}$. Indeed, $p(g)\in R=p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P)\rangle )$ as $p(f)\circ p(g)=p(f\circ g)\in p(\langle P\rangle )\subseteq \langle p(P)\rangle $. So $g=p(s)\in p(S^{p}_{R})$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: First inclusion, not using cartesianness

nodes.name: Converse inclusion: pick $g\in S^p_R$ with $s=p(g)$
nodes.statement: Conversely, let us show that $p(S^{p}_{R})\subseteq \langle p(f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle ))\rangle $. Given $s\in p(S^{p}_{R})$, we have an arrow $g\in S^{p}_{R}$ such that $s=p(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: Converse inclusion: pick $g\in S^p_R$ with $s=p(g)$

nodes.name: Claim: $g\in f^*(\langle P\rangle)$
nodes.statement: Let us show that $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$. Since $p(g)\in R=p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P)\rangle )$, $p(f)\circ p(g)=\xi\circ \gamma$ for some arrow $\xi\in P$ and some arrow $\gamma$. Now, since $\xi$ is cartesian (by our hypothesis every arrow of $P$ is cartesian), there is a unique arrow $\psi$ in $\cal C$ such that $p(\psi)=\gamma$ and $\xi\circ \psi=f\circ g$. So $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $g\in f^*(\langle P\rangle)$

nodes.name: Factor $p(f)\circ p(g)$ through an arrow of $P$
nodes.statement: Since $p(g)\in R=p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P)\rangle )$, $p(f)\circ p(g)=\xi\circ \gamma$ for some arrow $\xi\in P$ and some arrow $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $p(f)\circ p(g)$ through an arrow of $P$

nodes.name: Lift through the cartesian arrow $\xi$
nodes.statement: Now, since $\xi$ is cartesian (by our hypothesis every arrow of $P$ is cartesian), there is a unique arrow $\psi$ in $\cal C$ such that $p(\psi)=\gamma$ and $\xi\circ \psi=f\circ g$. So $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Lift through the cartesian arrow $\xi$

nodes.name: Prove (vii) from (iii) and (v)
nodes.statement: (vii) We know from (iii) that, if $P$ entirely consists of cartesian arrows then $\langle P\rangle =S^{p}_{\langle p(P)\rangle }$. We want to prove that if $g\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$ (equivalently, $f\circ g\in \langle P\rangle $) and we have a factorization $g=g'\circ h$ where $g'$ is cartesian and $h$ is vertical, then $g'\in f^{\ast}(\langle P\rangle )$ (equivalently, $f\circ g'\in \langle P\rangle $). But this follows from (v) (take $R=\langle p(P)\rangle $, $v$ is $h$ and $b$ is $f\circ g'$).
nodes.statement_short: Prove (vii) from (iii) and (v)

nodes.name: $\cal S$ satisfies maximality and multicomposition
nodes.statement: Let us first show that the collection $\cal S$ of sieves $R$ such that the collection of their cartesian arrows is sent by $p$ to a $K$-covering family defines a Grothendieck topology on $\cal C$. The maximality axiom is trivially satisfied; $\cal S$ is clearly closed under taking bigger sieves and under multicomposition of arrows (since $K$ is closed under taking bigger sieves and under multicomposition and the composite of two cartesian arrows is always a cartesian arrow). So it remains to prove that it satisfies the pullback stability property.
nodes.statement_short: $\cal S$ satisfies maximality and multicomposition; pullback-stability remains

nodes.name: Pullback-stability via Lemma 3.12(vii) and (vi)
nodes.statement: Given a sieve $R$ on an object $c$ and an arrow $f:c'\to c$ in $\cal C$, suppose that the presieve $P_{R}=\{f \mid f\in R \textup{ and } f \textup{ is cartesian}\}$ is sent by $p$ to a $K$-covering family. Then by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(vii) the sieve $f^{\ast}(\langle P_{R}\rangle )$ satisfies the property that all the cartesian images of the arrows in it lie again in it. Now, by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(vi), $f^{\ast}(\langle P_{R}\rangle )$ is sent by $p$ to a $K$-covering family, since the sieve generated by $p(f^{\ast}(\langle P_{R}\rangle ))$ is equal to the pullback sieve $p(f)^{\ast}(\langle p(P_{R})\rangle )$, which is $K$-covering since $\langle p(P_{R})\rangle $ is $K$-covering. It follows that the collection $(f^{\ast}(\langle P_{R}\rangle ))^{\textup{cart}}$ of cartesian images of arrows in $f^{\ast}(\langle P_{R}\rangle )$, which is contained, as we said, in $f^{\ast}(\langle P_{R}\rangle )$ and hence \emph{a fortiori} in $f^{\ast}(R)$, is sent by $p$ to a $K$-covering family. Therefore $f^{\ast}(R)$ lies in $\cal S$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Pullback-stability via Lemma 3.12(vii) and (vi)

nodes.name: $M^p_K\subseteq\cal S$ via Lemma 3.12(iv),(v)
nodes.statement: Now that we have proved that $\cal S$ is a Grothendieck topology on $\cal C$, it remains to show that it coincides with $M^{p}_{K}$. The fact that $M^{p}_{K}$ is contained in $\cal S$ follows from the fact that for any $K$-covering sieve $R$ on an object of the form $p(c)$, the sieve $S^{p}_{R}$ lies in $\cal S$ since, by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(iv), $R=\langle p(S^{p}_{R})\rangle $ and, by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(v), $S^{p}_{R}=\langle (S^{p}_{R})^{\textup{cart}}\rangle $, whence the collection $(S^{p}_{R})^{\textup{cart}}$, which is contained in $S^{p}_{R}$, is sent by $p$ to a $K$-covering family.
nodes.statement_short: $M^p_K\subseteq\cal S$ via Lemma 3.12(iv),(v)

nodes.name: ${\cal S}\subseteq M^p_K$ via Lemma 3.12(iii)
nodes.statement: To show the converse inclusion ${\cal S}\subseteq M^{p}_{K}$, it suffices to observe that, given a sieve $R$ in $\cal S$, the presieve $P_{R}$ consisting of the cartesian arrows in $R$ satisfies the property that $\langle p(P_{R})\rangle $ is $K$-covering; so the sieve $S^{p}_{\langle p(P_{R})\rangle }$ lies in $M^{p}_{K}$. But $S^{p}_{\langle p(P_{R})\rangle }=\langle P_{R}\rangle $ by Lemma \ref{lemmafibrations}(iii), so $\langle P_{R}\rangle $, and \emph{a fortiori} $R$, which contains it, is in $M^{p}_{K}$.
nodes.statement_short: ${\cal S}\subseteq M^p_K$ via Lemma 3.12(iii)

nodes.name: Cite Mac Lane-Moerdijk for (i)
nodes.statement: (i) This is Lemma 3(ii) at p. 410 of \cite{MM}.
nodes.statement_short: Cite Mac Lane-Moerdijk for (i)
nodes.section: 3.4 Relating morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $L_{y\circ G}\cong D_F$ preserves all limits, giving an essential morphism
nodes.statement: (ii) By definition of morphism of sites, $G$ is a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, T_{\cal D})\to ({\cal C}, T_{\cal C})$ if and only if the functor $L_{y_{\cal C}\circ G}:[{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ preserves finite limits. But $L_{y_{\cal C}\circ G}$ is left adjoint to $D_{G}:[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \to [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$. On the other hand, the adjunction $F\dashv G$ entails an adjunction $D_{F}:[{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \dashv D_{G}:[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \to [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, so, by the uniqueness (up to isomorphisms) of adjoints, we conclude that $L_{y_{\cal C}\circ G}\cong D_{F}$; in particular, it follows that $L_{y_{\cal C}\circ G}$ preserves arbitrary limits. So the geometric morphism $[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]\to [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ induced by $G$ is essential. The fact that the functor $y_{\cal C}\circ G$ is flat was also proved as Lemma 3(i) at p. 410 of \cite{MM}.
nodes.statement_short: $L_{y\circ G}\cong D_F$ preserves all limits, giving an essential morphism
nodes.section: 3.4 Relating morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Combine (i) and (ii)
nodes.statement: (iii) This follows immediately from (i) in light of (ii). Indeed, since $G$ is a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, T_{\cal D})\to ({\cal C}, T_{\cal C})$, it is a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ({\cal C}, J)$ if and only if it is cover-preserving.
nodes.statement_short: Combine (i) and (ii)
nodes.section: 3.4 Relating morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Inverse images agree since ${\rm Lan}_{G^{\rm op}}\cong D_F$
nodes.statement: (iv) By definition of geometric morphisms induced by a morphism or by a comorphism of sites, the inverse image of ${\bf Sh}(G)$ is the functor $a_{K}\circ \textup{Lan}_{G^{\textup{op}}}\circ i_{J}$, where $\textup{Lan}_{G^{\textup{op}}}$ is the left Kan extension functor along $G^{\textup{op}}$, while the inverse image of $C_{F}$ is $a_{K}\circ D_{F}\circ i_{J}$. Now, since $F\dashv G$, $D_{F}\dashv D_{G}$, whence $\textup{Lan}_{G^{\textup{op}}}\cong D_{F}$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Inverse images agree since ${\rm Lan}_{G^{\rm op}}\cong D_F$
nodes.section: 3.4 Relating morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi_{\cal C}\dashv i_F$
nodes.statement: (i) It is immediate to see that $\pi_{\cal C} \dashv i_{F}$. Let us show that $\pi_{\cal D}: ((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), T) \to ({\cal D}, K)$ is a morphism of sites, where $T$ is the trivial Grothendieck topology on $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)$. Notice that this will ensure that the collection of sieves $\tilde{K}$ defined in the statement of the theorem is indeed a Grothendieck topology, since it will be the Grothendieck topology induced by the morphism of sites $\pi_{\cal D}: ((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), T) \to ({\cal D}, K)$ (in the sense of Proposition \ref{reminducedtopology}).
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_{\cal C}\dashv i_F$; aim: $\pi_{\cal D}$ is a morphism of sites, so $\tilde K$ is a topology
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Deduce the conditions from those for $F$
nodes.statement: We will deduce that $\pi_{\cal D}:((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), T) \to ({\cal D}, K)$ satisfies properties (ii), (iii) and (iv) in the definition of morphism of sites (that is, Definition \ref{defmorphismsites}) from the fact that $F$ does.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce the conditions from those for $F$
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Condition (ii) for $\pi_{\cal D}$
nodes.statement: Let us start with condition (ii). Since $F:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal D}, K)$ satisfies it, every object $d$ of ${\mathcal D}$ admits a $K$-covering family $$ d_i \longrightarrow d \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ by objects $d_i$ of ${\mathcal D}$ which have morphisms $$ h_{i}:d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i) $$ to the images under $F$ of objects $c'_i$ of ${\mathcal C}$. Then we have, for each $i\in I$, an object $(c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i))$ of the category $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)$ and morphisms \[ d_{i}\to \pi_{\cal D}((c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i)))=d_{i} \] given by the identity arrows on the $d_{i}$. So $\pi_{\cal D}$ satisfies condition (ii) in the definition of morphism of sites.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (ii) for $\pi_{\cal D}$
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Condition (iii) for $\pi_{\cal D}$
nodes.statement: Let us now turn to condition (iii). Given objects $(c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1}))$ and $(c_{2}, d_{2}, \alpha_{2}:d_{2}\to F(c_{2}))$ and arrows $k_{1}:d\to \pi_{\cal D}((c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1})))=d_{1}$ and $k_{2}:d\to \pi_{\cal D}((c_{2}, d_{2}, \alpha_{2}:d_{2}\to F(c_{2})))=d_{2}$ in $\cal D$, consider the arrows $g_{1}:=\alpha_{1}\circ k_{1}:d\to F(c_{1})$ and $g_{2}:=\alpha_{2}\circ k_{2}:d\to F(c_{2})$. Then, since $F$ is a morphism of sites, there is a $K$-covering family $$ g'_i : d_i \longrightarrow d \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ and a family of pairs of morphisms of ${\mathcal C}$ $$ f_1^i : c'_i \longrightarrow c_1 \, , \quad f_2^i : c'_i \to c_2 \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ and of morphisms of ${\mathcal D}$ $$ h_i : d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i) \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ making the following squares commutative: $$ \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g'_i} \ar[d]_{h_i} & d \ar[d]^{g_1} \\ F(c'_i) \ar[r]^{F(f_1^i)} &F(c_1) } \qquad \qquad \qquad \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g'_i} \ar[d]_{h_i} & d \ar[d]^{g_2} \\ F(c'_i) \ar[r]^{F(f_2^i)} &F(c_2) } $$ These yield objects $(c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_{i}\to F(c'_i))$ of the category $1_{\cal D}\downarrow F$ (for $i\in I$) and arrows $$(f_1^i, k_{1}\circ g'_i):(c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_{i}\to F(c'_i)) \to (c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1}))$$ and $$(f_2^i, k_{2}\circ g'_i):(c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_{i}\to F(c'_i)) \to (c_{2}, d_{2}, \alpha_{1}:d_{2}\to F(c_{2}))$$ and morphisms of $\cal D$ \[ 1_{d_{i}}:d_{i}\to \pi_{\cal D}((c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_{i}\to F(c'_i)))=d_{i} \] (for each $i\in I$) making the following squares commutative: $$ \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g'_i} \ar[d]_{1_{d_{i}}} & d \ar[d]^{k_1} \\ d_{i} \ar[r]^{ k_{1}\circ g'_i} & d_{1} } \qquad \qquad \qquad \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g'_i} \ar[d]_{1_{d_{i}}} & d \ar[d]^{k_2} \\ d_{i} \ar[r]^{ k_{2}\circ g'_i} & d_{2} } $$ So $\pi_{\cal D}$ satisfies condition (iii) in the definition of morphism of sites.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (iii) for $\pi_{\cal D}$
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Condition (iv) for $\pi_{\cal D}$
nodes.statement: Lastly, let us consider condition (iv). Let $(f_{1}, k_{1}), (f_{2}, k_{2}):(c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1})) \rightrightarrows (c_{2}, d_{2}, \alpha_{2}:d_{2}\to F(c_{2}))$ be a pair of arrows in the category $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)$ and $z:d\to \pi_{\cal D}((c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1})))=d_{1}$ be an arrow of $\cal D$ satisfying \[ k_{1}\circ z=k_{2}\circ z. \] Let $g$ be the arrow $\alpha_{1}\circ z$. We have $F(f_{1})\circ g=F(f_{2})\circ g$. Indeed, $F(f_{1})\circ g=F(f_{1})\circ \alpha_{1}\circ z=\alpha_{2}\circ k_{1}\circ z=\alpha_{2}\circ k_{2}\circ z=F(f_{2})\circ \alpha_{1}\circ z=F(f_{2})\circ g$. So the fact that $F$ satisfies condition (iv) in the definition of morphism of sites ensures that there exist a $K$-covering family $$ g_i : d_i \longrightarrow d \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ and a family of morphisms of ${\mathcal C}$ $$ w_i : c'_i \longrightarrow c_{1} \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ satisfying $$ f_1 \circ w_i = f_2 \circ w_i \, , \quad \forall \, i \in I \, , $$ and of morphisms of ${\mathcal D}$ $$ h_i : d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i) \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ making the following squares commutative: $$ \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g_i} \ar[d]_{h_i} & d \ar[d]^{g} \\ F(c'_i) \ar[r]^{F(w_i)} & F(c_{1}) } $$ Then, for each $i\in I$, we have an object $(c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_i \to F(c'_i))$ of the category $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)$, and the commutativity of the above square ensures that $(w_{i}, z\circ g_{i})$ defines an arrow \[ (w_{i}, z\circ g_{i}):(c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_i \to F(c'_i)) \to (c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_1)) \] in $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)$. These arrows satisfy the property \[ (f_{1}, k_{1})\circ (w_{i}, z\circ g_{i}) = (f_{2}, k_{2})\circ (w_{i}, z\circ g_{i}) \] and the identity morphisms \[ 1_{d_{i}}:d_{i} \to \pi_{\cal D}((c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_i \to F(c'_i)))=d_{i} \] make the following squares commutative: $$ \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g_i} \ar[d]_{1_{d_{i}}} & d \ar[d]^{z} \\ d_{i} \ar[r]^{z\circ g_{i}} & d_{1} } $$ This shows that $\pi_{\cal D}$ satisfies condition (iv) in the definition of morphism of sites.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (iv) for $\pi_{\cal D}$
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi_{\cal D}$ is a comorphism of sites
nodes.statement: The functor $\pi_{\cal D}$ is also a comorphism of sites $((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K}) \to ({\cal D}, K)$. Indeed, given an object $(c, d, \alpha:d\to F(c))$ of $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)$ and a $K$-covering sieve $T$ on $\pi_{\cal D}((c, d, \alpha:d\to F(c)))=d$, the sieve generated by the family $\{(1_{c}, g):(c, \textup{dom}(g), \alpha\circ g: \textup{dom}(g) \to F(c)) \to (c, d, \alpha:d\to F(c)) \mid g\in T\}$ is $\tilde{K}$-covering and satisfies the required property since its image under $\pi_{\cal D}$ is precisely $T$.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_{\cal D}$ is a comorphism of sites
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Fullness and density give the equivalence by Proposition 7.18
nodes.statement: Next, let us show that $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $\tilde{K}$-full and $K$-dense. This will imply, by Proposition \ref{propmorphismcomorphismequivalence}, that it induces an equivalence of toposes ${\bf Sh}((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K}) \simeq {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)$ one half of which is the morphism $C_{\pi_{\cal D}}$ and whose other half is ${\bf Sh}(\pi_{\cal D})$.
nodes.statement_short: Fullness and density give the equivalence by Proposition 7.18
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $\tilde K$-full
nodes.statement: To show that $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $\tilde{K}$-full, let us consider an arrow $g$ in $\cal D$ from $\pi_{\cal D}((c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1})))=d_{1}$ to $\pi_{\cal D}((c_{2}, d_{2}, \alpha_{2}:d_{2}\to F(c_{2})))=d_{2}$. By applying condition (iii) in the definition of morphism of sites for $F$ to the arrows $\alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1})$ and $\alpha_{2}\circ g:d_{1}\to F(c_{2})$ we obtain a $K$-covering family $$ g'_i : d_i \longrightarrow d_1 \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ and a family of pairs of morphisms of ${\mathcal C}$ $$ f_1^i : c'_i \longrightarrow c_1 \, , \quad f_2^i : c'_i \to c_2 \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ and of morphisms of ${\mathcal D}$ $$ h_i : d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i) \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ making the following squares commutative: $$ \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g'_i} \ar[d]_{h_i} & d_1 \ar[d]^{\alpha_{1}} \\ F(c'_i) \ar[r]^{F(f_1^i)} &F(c_1) } \qquad \qquad \qquad \xymatrix{ d_i \ar[r]^{g'_i} \ar[d]_{h_i} & d_1 \ar[d]^{\alpha_{2}\circ g} \\ F(c'_i) \ar[r]^{F(f_2^i)} &F(c_2) } $$ Now, the commutativity of these squares ensures that we have, for each $i\in I$, arrows \[ (f_1^i, g'_i):(c'_i, d_i, h_i:d_i \to F(c'_i)) \to (c_{1}, d_{1}, \alpha_{1}:d_{1}\to F(c_{1})) \] and \[ (f_2^i, g\circ g'_i):(c'_i, d_i, h_i:d_i \to F(c'_i)) \to (c_{2}, d_{2}, \alpha_{2}:d_{2}\to F(c_{2})) \] arrows in the category $1_{\cal D}\downarrow F$. These arrows clearly satisfy the condition \[ g\circ \pi_{\cal D}((f_1^i, g'_i))=\pi_{\cal D}((f_2^i, g\circ g'_i)), \] and the family $\{(f_1^i, g'_i) \mid i\in I\}$ is $\tilde{K}$-covering (since $\{ g'_i \mid i\in I \}$ is $K$-covering). This shows that $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $\tilde{K}$-full, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $\tilde K$-full
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $K$-dense
nodes.statement: Let us now prove that $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $K$-dense. Given $d\in {\cal D}$, using the fact that $F$ satisfies condition (ii) in the definition of morphism of sites, we obtain a $K$-covering family $$ d_i \longrightarrow d \, , \quad i \in I \, , $$ by objects $d_i$ of ${\mathcal D}$ which have morphisms $$ h_{i}:d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i) $$ to the images under $F$ of objects $c'_i$ of ${\mathcal C}$. Since we can write $d_{i}=\pi_{\cal D}(c'_i, d_{i}, h_{i}:d_i \longrightarrow F(c'_i))$, it follows that $d$ can be $K$-covered by objects in the image of the functor $\pi_{\cal D}$, which proves that this functor is $K$-dense, as required.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_{\cal D}$ is $K$-dense
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi_{\cal C}$ is a comorphism of sites
nodes.statement: Let us now show that $\pi_{\cal C}$ is a comorphism of sites $((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K}) \to ({\cal C}, J)$. Given a sieve $S$ on an object of the form $\pi_{\cal C}(c, d, \alpha:d\to F(c))=c$, since $F$ is cover-preserving, the family $\{F(f) \mid f\in S\}$ is $K$-covering on $F(c)$ and hence the pullback $\alpha^{\ast}(R)$ along $\alpha$ of the sieve $R$ generated by it is $K$-covering on $d$. So, for any $g\in \alpha^{\ast}(R)$, there is an element $i_{g}\in I$ and an arrow $\beta_{g}:\textup{dom}(g)\to F(\textup{dom}(f_{i_{g}}))$ such that $\alpha \circ g=F(\textup{dom}(f_{i_{g}}))\circ \beta_{g}$. So the sieve generated by the family of arrows \[ (f_{i_{g}}, g):(\textup{dom}(f_{i_{g}}), \textup{dom}(g), \beta_{g}: \textup{dom}(g) \to F(\textup{dom}(f_{i_{g}}))) \to (c, d, \alpha:d\to F(c)) \] satisfies the required property since its image under $\pi_{\cal C}$ is contained in $S$.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_{\cal C}$ is a comorphism of sites
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $i_F$ is a morphism of sites by Proposition 3.14(iii)
nodes.statement: Since $\pi_{\cal C}$ is a comorphism of sites $((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K}) \to ({\cal C}, J)$ and $\pi_{\cal C} \dashv i_{F}$, it thus follows from Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(iii) that $i_{F}$ is a morphism of sites $({\cal C}, J)\to ((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})$.
nodes.statement_short: $i_F$ is a morphism of sites by Proposition 3.14(iii)
nodes.section: 3.4.1 From morphisms to comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: $j_F$, $\pi'_{\cal C}$ are comorphisms and $j_F$ is a dense morphism
nodes.statement: (i) It is clear that $j_{F}\dashv \pi_{\cal D}'$ and that $\pi_{\cal C}'\circ j_{F}=F$. Since $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is cover-preserving, it follows from Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(i) that $j_{F}$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((F \downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})$. The fact that $\pi_{\cal C}'$ is a comorphism of sites $((F \downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})\to ({\cal C}, J)$ follows from the fact that $F:({\cal D}, K)\to ({\cal C}, J)$ is. Indeed, given an object $(c,d, \alpha:F(d)\to c)$ of the category $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$ and a $J$-covering sieve $S$ on $\pi_{\cal C}'((d, c, \alpha:F(d)\to c))=c$, $\alpha^{\ast}(S)$ is $J$-covering on $F(d)$ and hence contains the image under $F$ of a $K$-covering sieve $R$ on $d$. We thus have, for each $g\in R$, an arrow $f_{g}:F(\textup{dom}(g))\to c$ in $S$ such that $\alpha \circ F(g)=f_{g}$. The family $\{ (g, f_{g}):(\textup{dom}(g), F(\textup{dom}(g)), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(g))} ) \to (d, c, \alpha:F(d)\to c) \mid g\in R\}$ is therefore $\overline{K}$-covering and its image under $\pi_{\cal C}'$ is contained in $S$. It is clear that $j_{F}$ is full and faithful and cover-preserving, so to conclude that it is a dense morphism of sites, it suffices to show that it is $\overline{K}$-dense. But this follows from the following observation: for any object $(d,c, \alpha:F(d)\to c)$ of the category $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$, the arrow $(1_{d}, \alpha):(d, F(d), 1_{F(d)}:F(d)\to F(d)) \to (d,c, \alpha:F(d)\to c)$ is $\overline{K}$-covering.
nodes.statement_short: $j_F$, $\pi'_{\cal C}$ are comorphisms and $j_F$ is a dense morphism
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is a morphism and comorphism inducing an equivalence
nodes.statement: (ii) The fact that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is a morphism of sites $((F \downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})\to ({\cal D}, K)$ follows from the fact that its left adjoint $j_{F}$ is by (i) a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((F \downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})$ in light of Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(iii). Let us show that it is also a comorphism of sites. Given an object $(c,d, \alpha:F(d)\to c)$ of the category $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$ and a $K$-covering sieve $T$ on $d$, the family $\{(\textup{dom}(g), 1_{c}, \alpha\circ F(g):F(\textup{dom}(g))\to c \mid g\in T\}$ is $\overline{K}$-covering and its image under $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is contained in $T$. By Proposition \ref{propmorphismcomorphismequivalence}, to show that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ induces an equivalence of toposes as in the statement of the theorem, it suffices to show that it is $K$-dense and $\overline{K}$-full. Since $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is surjective (for any $d\in {\cal D}$, $d=\pi_{\cal D}'((d, F(d), 1_{F(d)}))$), it is \emph{a fortiori} $K$-dense. To show that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is $\overline{K}$-full, consider two objects $(d_{1}, c_{1}, \alpha_{1}:F(d_{1})\to c_{1})$ and $(d_{2}, c_{2}, \alpha_{2}:F(d_{2})\to c_{2})$ of the category $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$ and an arrow $g:d_{1}\to d_{2}$ in $\cal D$. Then we have a $\overline{K}$-covering arrow $$(1_{d_{1}}, \alpha_{1}):(d_{1}, F(d_{1}), 1_{F(d_{1})}:F(d_{1})\to F(d_{1}))\to (d_{1}, c_{1}, \alpha_{1}:F(d_{1})\to c_{1})$$ (its image under $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is the identity arrow on $d_{1}$) and an arrow $$(g, \alpha_{2}\circ F(g)):(d_{1}, F(d_{1}), 1_{F(d_{1})}:F(d_{1})\to F(d_{1}))\to (d_{2}, c_{2}, \alpha_{2}:F(d_{2})\to c_{2})$$ in $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$ satisfying the condition \[ \pi_{\cal D}'((g, \alpha_{2}\circ F(g)))=g\circ \pi_{\cal D}'((1_{d_{1}}, \alpha_{1})). \] This shows that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is $\overline{K}$-full, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is a morphism and comorphism inducing an equivalence
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is a morphism of sites by Proposition 3.14(iii)
nodes.statement: (ii) The fact that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is a morphism of sites $((F \downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})\to ({\cal D}, K)$ follows from the fact that its left adjoint $j_{F}$ is by (i) a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((F \downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})$ in light of Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(iii).
nodes.statement_short: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is a morphism of sites by Proposition 3.14(iii)
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is a comorphism of sites
nodes.statement: Let us show that it is also a comorphism of sites. Given an object $(c,d, \alpha:F(d)\to c)$ of the category $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$ and a $K$-covering sieve $T$ on $d$, the family $\{(\textup{dom}(g), 1_{c}, \alpha\circ F(g):F(\textup{dom}(g))\to c \mid g\in T\}$ is $\overline{K}$-covering and its image under $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is contained in $T$.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is a comorphism of sites
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: Reduce to density and fullness
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{propmorphismcomorphismequivalence}, to show that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ induces an equivalence of toposes as in the statement of the theorem, it suffices to show that it is $K$-dense and $\overline{K}$-full. Since $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is surjective (for any $d\in {\cal D}$, $d=\pi_{\cal D}'((d, F(d), 1_{F(d)}))$), it is \emph{a fortiori} $K$-dense.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to density and fullness; density is immediate
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is $\overline K$-full
nodes.statement: To show that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is $\overline{K}$-full, consider two objects $(d_{1}, c_{1}, \alpha_{1}:F(d_{1})\to c_{1})$ and $(d_{2}, c_{2}, \alpha_{2}:F(d_{2})\to c_{2})$ of the category $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$ and an arrow $g:d_{1}\to d_{2}$ in $\cal D$. Then we have a $\overline{K}$-covering arrow $$(1_{d_{1}}, \alpha_{1}):(d_{1}, F(d_{1}), 1_{F(d_{1})}:F(d_{1})\to F(d_{1}))\to (d_{1}, c_{1}, \alpha_{1}:F(d_{1})\to c_{1})$$ (its image under $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is the identity arrow on $d_{1}$) and an arrow $$(g, \alpha_{2}\circ F(g)):(d_{1}, F(d_{1}), 1_{F(d_{1})}:F(d_{1})\to F(d_{1}))\to (d_{2}, c_{2}, \alpha_{2}:F(d_{2})\to c_{2})$$ in $(F \downarrow 1_{\cal C})$ satisfying the condition \[ \pi_{\cal D}'((g, \alpha_{2}\circ F(g)))=g\circ \pi_{\cal D}'((1_{d_{1}}, \alpha_{1})). \] This shows that $\pi_{\cal D}'$ is $\overline{K}$-full, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi'_{\cal D}$ is $\overline K$-full
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: $m_F$ is a morphism of sites
nodes.statement: (iii) We know that the functor $m_{F}:{\cal C}\to [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ sending an object $c$ of $\cal C$ to the presheaf $\textup{Hom}_{\cal D}(F(-), c)$ is flat and that its composite with the associated sheaf functor $a_{K}:[{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]\to {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)$ is $J$-continuous. So we can regard $m_{F}$ as a morphism of sites $({\cal C}, J)\to (\hat{\cal D}, \hat{K})$. The fact that the triangle in the statement of the theorem commutes follows from Proposition \ref{propyonedamorcomor} and the fact that $a_{K}\circ m_{F}$ is the flat functor corresponding via Diaconescu's equivalence to the geometric morphism $C_{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: $m_F$ is a morphism of sites; triangle commutes
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: Part (i) from Theorems 3.16 and 3.18
nodes.statement: (i) The fact that $w_{F}$ is both a morphism and a comorphism of sites $((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K}) \to ((c_{F}\downarrow 1_{\cal D}), \overline{\tilde{K}})$ inducing equivalences which make the diagram in the statement of the theorem commute follows from the equality $\pi_{\cal D}'''\circ w_{F}=\pi_{\cal D}$ in light of Theorems \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism} and \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}. The fact that $w_{F}=j_{c_{F}}$ is full and faithful and a dense morphism of sites follows from Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}.
nodes.statement_short: Part (i) from Theorems 3.16 and 3.18
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: Part (ii) from the same theorems and density of representables
nodes.statement: (ii) The fact that $z_{G}$ is both a morphism and a comorphism of sites $((G\downarrow 1_{\cal C}), \overline{K})\to ((1_{\hat{\cal D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}} )$ inducing equivalences making the diagram in the statement of the theorem commute follows from the equality $\pi_{\hat{\cal D}}\circ z_{G}=y_{\cal D}\circ \pi_{\cal D}'$ in light of Theorems \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism} and \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}. It is clear that $z_{G}$ is full and faithful, so it remains to show that it is $\widetilde{\hat{K}}$-dense. But this easily follows from the fact that every presheaf on $\cal D$ is $\hat{K}$-covered by representables.
nodes.statement_short: Part (ii) from the same theorems and density of representables
nodes.section: 3.4.2 From comorphisms to morphisms of sites

nodes.name: Set up $c_F$, $m_{c_F}$ and the functor $\xi_F$
nodes.statement: Let us define the unit $\eta$ and counit $\epsilon$ of the dual adjunction. Given a morphism of sites $F:({\cal C}, J)\to ({\cal D}, K)$, the corresponding comorphism of sites $c_{F}:((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})\to ({\cal C}, J)$ is given by the canonical projection functor $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)\to {\cal C}$. The morphism of sites associated with $c_{F}$ is \[ m_{c_{F}}:({\cal C}, J)\to (\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}}), \] where $m_{c_{F}}(c)=\textup{Hom}_{\cal C}(c_{F}(-), c)$ (for any $c\in {\cal C}$). Let us define $\xi_{F}:{\cal D}\to \widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}$ as the functor sending any object $d\in {\cal D}$ to the presheaf $\textup{Hom}_{\cal D}(\pi_{\cal D}(-), d)$, where $\pi_{\cal D}$ is the canonical projection functor $(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)\to {\cal D}$, and acting on the arrows in the obvious way. The functor $\xi_{F}$ yields a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to (\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}})$, since it is precisely the morphism of sites $m_{\pi_{\cal D}}$ associated as in Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}(iii) with the comorphism of sites $\pi_{\cal D}:((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})\to ({\cal D}, K)$ (note that $\pi_{\cal D}$ is indeed a comorphism of such sites by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii)).
nodes.statement_short: Set up $c_F$, $m_{c_F}$ and the functor $\xi_F$
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Claim: the triangle commutes after applying ${\bf Sh}$
nodes.statement: Let us check that, whilst \emph{not} necessarily commuting at the level of morphisms of sites, the diagram \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} ({\cal C}, J) \arrow[rr, "m_{c_{F}}"] \arrow[drr, "F"] & & (\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \hat{\tilde{K}}) \\ & & ({\cal D}, K) \ar[u, "\xi_{F}"] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} {\flushleft commutes after applying the functor ${\bf Sh}$ to it, i.e. ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})$.}
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the triangle commutes after applying ${\bf Sh}$
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Verify the claim using Theorems 3.18(iii) and 3.16(ii)
nodes.statement: Since $C_{y_{{\cal D}'}}:{\bf Sh}((1_{\cal D}\downarrow F), \tilde{K})\to {\bf Sh}(\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}})$ is an equivalence (cf. Proposition \ref{propyonedamorcomor}), to show that ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})$ it is equivalent to prove that ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ {\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}} \cong {\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}$. Now, by Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}(iii), ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}={\bf Sh}(m_{\pi_{\cal D}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}} \cong C_{\pi_{\cal D}}$ and ${\bf Sh}(m_{c_{F}})\circ C_{y_{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}}\cong C_{c_{F}}$. But ${\bf Sh}(F)\circ C_{\pi_{\cal D}}\cong C_{c_{F}}$ by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii), as required.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the claim using Theorems 3.18(iii) and 3.16(ii)
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: ${\bf Sh}(\xi_F)$ is an equivalence
nodes.statement: The morphism ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F}):{\bf Sh}(\widehat{(1_{\cal D}\downarrow F)}, \widehat{\tilde{K}})\to {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)$ is actually an equivalence. Indeed, by Theorem \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}(iii), ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})={\bf Sh}(m_{c_{\pi_{\cal D}}})$ is an equivalence if and only if $C_{c_{\pi_{\cal D}}}$ is, and by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii), $C_{c_{\pi_{\cal D}}}$ is an equivalence if and only if ${\bf Sh}(\pi_{\cal D})$ is, which is the case by Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(ii). We set the component $\epsilon_{F}:m_{c_{F}} \to F$ at $F$ of the counit $\epsilon$ of our adjunction equal to the geometric morphism ${\bf Sh}(\xi_{F})$ (note that this is actually an arrow $F\to m_{c_{F}}$ in ${\textup{\bf Mor}}_{({\cal C}, J)}$, that is, an arrow $m_{c_{F}} \to F$ in $({\textup{\bf Mor}}_{({\cal C}, J)})^{\textup{op}}$).
nodes.statement_short: ${\bf Sh}(\xi_F)$ is an equivalence; define the counit
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Define the unit via the comorphism $\chi_G=z_G\circ j_G$
nodes.statement: Let us now define the unit of our dual adjunction. Let $G$ be a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to ({\cal C}, J)$. The comorphism of sites $c_{m_{G}}:((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}})\to ({\cal C}, J)$ associated with the morphism of sites $m_{G}:({\cal C}, J)\to (\hat{D}, \hat{K})$ via Theorem \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism}(iii) is given by the canonical projection functor $(1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}) \to {\cal C}$. We define the component $\eta_{G}:G\to c_{m_{G}}$ of the unit at $G$ as the geometric morphism \[ C_{\chi_{G}}:{\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)\to {\bf Sh}((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}}) \] induced by the comorphism of sites \[ \chi_{G}:({\cal D}, K)\to ((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}}) \] given by the functor ${\cal D}\to (1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G})$ sending any object $d$ of $\cal D$ to the object $(y_{\cal D}(d), G(c), \alpha:y_{\cal D}(d)\to m_{G}(G(d))$, where $\alpha$ is the natural transformation corresponding to the identity on $G(d)$, regarded as an element of $m_{G}(G(d))(d)$, via the Yoneda lemma. Notice that $\chi_{G}$ is indeed a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to ((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}})$, since $\chi_{G}=z_{G}\circ j_{G}$, where $j_{G}$ and $z_{G}$ are the comorphisms of sites considered in Theorem \ref{thmtoposadjunction}(ii). Moreover, $C_{\chi_{G}}$ is an equivalence, since, by that theorem, both $C_{j_{G}}$ and $C_{z_{G}}$ are.
nodes.statement_short: Define the unit via the comorphism $\chi_G=z_G\circ j_G$
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: The triangle of comorphisms commutes
nodes.statement: The diagram \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} ({\cal D}, K) \arrow[rr, "G"] \ar[d, "\chi_{G}"] & & ({\cal C}, J) \\ ((1_{\hat{D}}\downarrow m_{G}), \widetilde{\hat{K}}) \ar[urr, "c_{m_{G}}"{below, xshift=1.5ex}] & & \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} {\flushleft of comorphisms of sites clearly commutes (without the need of applying the functor $C$ to it).} The verification that the unit and counit satisfy the triangular identities is an immediate consequence of their definition in light of the commutativity of the diagrams in Theorems \ref{thmmorphismtocomorphism} and \ref{thmcomorphismtomorphism}; the details are straightforward and left to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: The triangle of comorphisms commutes; triangular identities are routine
nodes.section: 3.4.3 The dual adjunction between morphisms and comorphisms of sites

nodes.name: Part (i): adjunction and covering-lifting
nodes.statement: (i) The fact that $\pi_{\cal D}^{F} \dashv i_{F}'$ is clear. By definition of coinduced topology $K^{i_{F}'}$, $i_{F}'$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'})$, which is also cover-preserving ($i_{F}'$ being full). So, by Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(i), its left adjoint $\pi_{\cal D}^{F}$ is a comorphism of sites $((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'}) \to ({\cal D}, K)$ and $i_{F}'$ is a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'})$. It remains to show that $\pi_{\cal C}^{F}$ is a comorphism of sites ${\bf Sh}((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'}) \to ({\cal C}, J)$. Let $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ be an object of $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$, and let us suppose that $R$ is a $J$-covering sieve on the object $c=\pi_{\cal C}^{F}((c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d)))$. Let $\tilde{R}$ be the sieve in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ on $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ generated by by the arrows of the form $(f, 1_{d}):(\textup{dom}(f), d, \alpha\circ f:\textup{dom}(f) \to F(d))\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$. Clearly, the image of $\tilde{R}$ under $\pi_{\cal C}^{F}$ is contained in $R$, so if we show that $\tilde{R}$ is $K^{i_{F}'}$-covering, we are done. Now, $\tilde{R}$ is $K^{i_{F}'}$-covering if and only if for any arrow $\xi=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})$ in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ to $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ from an object of the form $i_{F}'(d')=(F(d'),d', 1_{F(d')})$, $\xi^{\ast}(\tilde{R})$ contains the image under $i_{F}'$ of a $K$-covering sieve on $d'$. Notice that, since $\xi=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})$ is an arrow $(F(d'),d', 1_{F(d')})\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$, we have $\alpha\circ \xi_{1}=F(\xi_{2})$. Consider the sieve $\xi_{1}^{\ast}(R)$ on $F(d')$; it is $J$-covering as it is the pullback of a $J$-covering sieve. So, since $F$ is, by our hypothesis, a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to ({\cal C}, J)$, there is a $K$-covering sieve $T$ on $d'$ such that $F(T)\subseteq \xi_{1}^{\ast}(R)$. Let us show that $i_{F}'(T)\subseteq \xi^{\ast}(\tilde{R})$. For any $t\in T$, $\xi\circ i_{F}'(t)=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})\circ (F(t), t)=(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)),\textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}) \to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$. But $\xi_{1}\circ F(t)\in R$ and hence the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), 1_{d}):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t): F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ lies in $\tilde{R}$. But the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ can be written as the composite of this arrow with the arrow $(1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}, \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), \textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))})\to (F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t):F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))$, which is indeed an arrow in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ since $F(\xi_{2}\circ t)=\alpha \circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t)$ (this follows from the previously remarked fact that $\alpha\circ \xi_{1}=F(\xi_{2})$). So $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ also lies in $\tilde{R}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Part (i): adjunction and covering-lifting
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Proposition 3.14 handles $\pi^F_{\cal D}$ and $i'_F$
nodes.statement: (i) The fact that $\pi_{\cal D}^{F} \dashv i_{F}'$ is clear. By definition of coinduced topology $K^{i_{F}'}$, $i_{F}'$ is a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'})$, which is also cover-preserving ($i_{F}'$ being full). So, by Proposition \ref{propadjointinduction}(i), its left adjoint $\pi_{\cal D}^{F}$ is a comorphism of sites $((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'}) \to ({\cal D}, K)$ and $i_{F}'$ is a morphism of sites $({\cal D}, K) \to ((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'})$. It remains to show that $\pi_{\cal C}^{F}$ is a comorphism of sites ${\bf Sh}((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), K^{i_{F}'}) \to ({\cal C}, J)$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3.14 handles $\pi^F_{\cal D}$ and $i'_F$; it remains to treat $\pi^F_{\cal C}$
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Define the sieve $\tilde R$ and reduce to its being covering
nodes.statement: Let $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ be an object of $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$, and let us suppose that $R$ is a $J$-covering sieve on the object $c=\pi_{\cal C}^{F}((c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d)))$. Let $\tilde{R}$ be the sieve in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ on $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ generated by by the arrows of the form $(f, 1_{d}):(\textup{dom}(f), d, \alpha\circ f:\textup{dom}(f) \to F(d))\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$. Clearly, the image of $\tilde{R}$ under $\pi_{\cal C}^{F}$ is contained in $R$, so if we show that $\tilde{R}$ is $K^{i_{F}'}$-covering, we are done. Now, $\tilde{R}$ is $K^{i_{F}'}$-covering if and only if for any arrow $\xi=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})$ in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ to $(c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ from an object of the form $i_{F}'(d')=(F(d'),d', 1_{F(d')})$, $\xi^{\ast}(\tilde{R})$ contains the image under $i_{F}'$ of a $K$-covering sieve on $d'$. Notice that, since $\xi=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})$ is an arrow $(F(d'),d', 1_{F(d')})\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$, we have $\alpha\circ \xi_{1}=F(\xi_{2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the sieve $\tilde R$ and reduce to its being covering
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Use that $F$ is a comorphism to get a covering $T$
nodes.statement: Consider the sieve $\xi_{1}^{\ast}(R)$ on $F(d')$; it is $J$-covering as it is the pullback of a $J$-covering sieve. So, since $F$ is, by our hypothesis, a comorphism of sites $({\cal D}, K)\to ({\cal C}, J)$, there is a $K$-covering sieve $T$ on $d'$ such that $F(T)\subseteq \xi_{1}^{\ast}(R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Use that $F$ is a comorphism to get a covering $T$
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Claim: $i'_F(T)\subseteq\xi^*(\tilde R)$
nodes.statement: Let us show that $i_{F}'(T)\subseteq \xi^{\ast}(\tilde{R})$. For any $t\in T$, $\xi\circ i_{F}'(t)=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})\circ (F(t), t)=(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)),\textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}) \to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$. But $\xi_{1}\circ F(t)\in R$ and hence the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), 1_{d}):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t): F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ lies in $\tilde{R}$. But the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ can be written as the composite of this arrow with the arrow $(1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}, \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), \textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))})\to (F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t):F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))$, which is indeed an arrow in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ since $F(\xi_{2}\circ t)=\alpha \circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t)$ (this follows from the previously remarked fact that $\alpha\circ \xi_{1}=F(\xi_{2})$). So $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ also lies in $\tilde{R}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $i'_F(T)\subseteq\xi^*(\tilde R)$
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Compute $\xi\circ i'_F(t)$
nodes.statement: For any $t\in T$, $\xi\circ i_{F}'(t)=(\xi_{1}, \xi_{2})\circ (F(t), t)=(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)),\textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}) \to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\xi\circ i'_F(t)$
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Factor through an arrow of $\tilde R$
nodes.statement: But $\xi_{1}\circ F(t)\in R$ and hence the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), 1_{d}):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t): F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))\to (c, d, \alpha:c\to F(d))$ lies in $\tilde{R}$. But the arrow $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ can be written as the composite of this arrow with the arrow $(1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))}, \xi_{2}\circ t):(F(\textup{dom}(t)), \textup{dom}(t), 1_{F(\textup{dom}(t))})\to (F(\textup{dom}(t)), d, \alpha\circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t):F(\textup{dom}(t))\to F(d))$, which is indeed an arrow in $(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)$ since $F(\xi_{2}\circ t)=\alpha \circ \xi_{1}\circ F(t)$ (this follows from the previously remarked fact that $\alpha\circ \xi_{1}=F(\xi_{2})$).
nodes.statement_short: Factor through an arrow of $\tilde R$
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Conclude the claim
nodes.statement: So $(\xi_{1}\circ F(t), \xi_{2}\circ t)$ also lies in $\tilde{R}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the claim
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Part (ii) via Proposition 7.18: $i'_F$ is full and dense
nodes.statement: (ii) To show that $i_{F}'$ induces equivalences in the statement of the theorem, by Proposition \ref{propmorphismcomorphismequivalence} we are reduced, in light of (i), to prove that it is $K$-full and $K^{i_{F}'}$-dense. The functor $i_{F}'$ is actually full, so \emph{a fortiori} $K$-full, and it is $K^{i_{F}'}$-dense by Proposition \ref{propimagetopology}.
nodes.statement_short: Part (ii) via Proposition 7.18: $i'_F$ is full and dense
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 3.13
nodes.statement: (i) This is an immediate consequence of Theorem \ref{thmfibration1}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 3.13
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Pullback lemma for subtoposes
nodes.statement: (ii) This follows from the ($2$-dimensional) pullback lemma, which implies that the left-hand square in the following diagram (where the unnamed vertical arrows are the canonical geometric inclusions) is a pullback (since the right-hand square and the outer rectangle are): $$ \xymatrix{ {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, M^{J}_{F}) \ar[d] \ar[r] & {\bf Sh}((1_{\cal C}\downarrow F), M^{\pi^{F}_{\cal C}}_{J}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[d]^{C_{F}} \\ [{\cal D}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{C_{i_{F}'}\quad} & [(1_{\cal C}\downarrow F)^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \ar[r]^{\quad C_{\pi^{F}_{\cal C}}} & [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] } $$ (notice that the composite of the lower horizontal arrows is $C_{F}$).
nodes.statement_short: Pullback lemma for subtoposes
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Combine (ii) with Theorem 3.7
nodes.statement: (iii) This follows from (ii) and Theorem \ref{thmcorrespondenceinclusion}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine (ii) with Theorem 3.7
nodes.section: 3.4.4 The fibration of generalized elements of a functor

nodes.name: Counit components are epimorphisms
nodes.statement: (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii). Since $R$ is faithful, for any object $e$ of $\cal E$, the component $\epsilon_{e}:L(R(e))\to e$ of the counit of the adjunction $L\dashv R$ is an epimorphism. So condition (ii) is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Counit components are epimorphisms

nodes.name: Epimorphisms $L(u)\to e$ factor through the counit
nodes.statement: (ii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i). Any arrow $\alpha:L(u)\to e$, $\alpha$ factors through the component $\epsilon_{e}$ at $e$ of counit of the adjunction $L\dashv R$. So if $\alpha:L(u)\to e$ is an epimorphism, $\epsilon_{e}$ is also an epimorphism. Since this holds for every $e$, it implies that $R$ is faithful.
nodes.statement_short: Epimorphisms $L(u)\to e$ factor through the counit

nodes.name: Reduce to separating sets
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the last assertion of the proposition. The fact that it suffices to require condition (ii) for every $e$ in $\cal C$ follows from the fact that every object $e$ of $\cal E$ admits an epimorphic family from objects in $\cal C$. On the other hand, since $\cal D$ is separating for $\cal F$, requiring, for a given object $c$, that there should be an epimorphism $L(u)\to c$, is equivalent to the condition that the family of all arrows $L(d)\to c$ (where $d\in {\cal D}$) is epimorphic (since $L$ preserves colimits, having a right adjoint, and hence epimorphic families).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to separating sets

nodes.name: Easy implications
nodes.statement: The implications (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (ii) and (i) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (iii) are clear. The fact that, in (iii), if the factorization exists then it is unique (up to isomorphism) can be proved as follows.
nodes.statement_short: Easy implications; prove uniqueness of the factorization

nodes.name: The factor $r$ preserves colimits and has a right adjoint $j$
nodes.statement: Since $i^{\ast}\circ i_{\ast}\cong 1_{\cal F}$ and $i^{\ast}$ preserves colimits, if $f^{\ast}$ factors as $r\circ i^{\ast}$ then the functor $r$ preserves colimits and hence has a right adjoint; let us call it $j$.
nodes.statement_short: The factor $r$ preserves colimits and has a right adjoint $j$

nodes.name: Pass to right adjoints to conclude
nodes.statement: Now, since $f^{\ast}\cong r\circ i^{\ast}$, passing to the right adjoints we obtain that $f_{\ast}\cong i_{\ast}\circ j$; in other words, $f_{\ast}$ factors (necessarily uniquely up to isomorphism) through $i_{\ast}$ and $j$ identifies with this factorization. So $r$ is uniquely determined as the left adjoint to this factorization. This argument actually proves that (iii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i). Similarly, we can prove that (ii) $\!\Rightarrow\!$ (i).
nodes.statement_short: Pass to right adjoints to conclude

nodes.name: Unfold the definition
nodes.statement: By definition, $A$ is $(J, K)$-continuous if and only if the functor \[ R_{l'\circ A}:{\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)\to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }] \] takes values in ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\subseteq [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold the definition

nodes.name: Identify $R_{l'\circ A}\cong D_A\circ i_K$
nodes.statement: But we have \[ R_{l'\circ A} \cong D_{A}\circ i_{K}. \] Indeed, for any $E\in {\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)$, \[ R_{l'\circ A}(E)= \textup{Hom}_{{\bf Sh}({\cal D}, K)}((l'\circ A)(-), E)\cong E\circ A^{\textup{op}}=(D_{A}\circ i_{K})(E) \] naturally in $E$. From this our thesis immediately follows.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $R_{l'\circ A}\cong D_A\circ i_K$

nodes.name: (i),(ii): sheaf condition for $R_A(e)$ is the colimit condition
nodes.statement: (i) and (ii) are immediate, since stating that all the functors of the form $R_{A}(e)=\textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(A(-), e)$ (for $e\in {\cal E}$) satisfy the sheaf condition with respect to a sieve $S$ on an object $c$ amounts precisely to saying that $A(c)=\varinjlim_{f:d\to c \in S} A(d)$.
nodes.statement_short: (i),(ii): sheaf condition for $R_A(e)$ is the colimit condition

nodes.name: (iii): colimit implies epimorphic
nodes.statement: (iii) The equality $A(c)=\varinjlim_{f:d\to c \in S} A(d)$ implies in particular that the family of arrows $\{A(\textup{dom}(f)) \to A(c) \mid f\in S\}$ is epimorphic, i.e. that $A$ is $J$-continuous. If $A$ is flat then the geometric morphism $(L_{A}\dashv R_{A})$ factors through the canonical inclusion ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ if and only if $A$ is $J$-continuous (see, for instance, Corollary 4 at p. 394 of \cite{MM}). The second assertion, about morphisms of sites, follows from the first about flat functors by Remark \ref{remmorphismsofsites}(a).
nodes.statement_short: (iii): colimit implies epimorphic; flat case via Mac Lane-Moerdijk

nodes.name: (iv): largest topology making given presheaves sheaves
nodes.statement: (iv) This follows from the fact that, for any collection $\cal P$ of presheaves on a given category $\cal C$, there is a largest Grothendieck topology for which all of them are sheaves. This topology can be explicitly characterized as the topology having as covering sieves precisely the sieves $S$ such that every presheaf $P$ in $\cal P$ satisfies the sheaf condition with respect to all the pullback sieves $g^{\ast}(S)$ (see, for instance, the proof of Proposition C2.1.9 \cite{El}). If $\cal P$ is the class of presheaves in the image of the functor $R_{A}$ then this condition amounts precisely to requiring that for any arrow $g:d\to c$, $A(d)=\varinjlim_{h:e\to d \in g^{\ast}(S)} A(e)$ (cf. the proof of (i)).
nodes.statement_short: (iv): largest topology making given presheaves sheaves

nodes.name: Quasi-inverse assignments via Yoneda
nodes.statement: (i) One half of the equivalence is given by the assignment $A \mapsto (L_{A}\dashv R_{A})$; the other half sends a weak morphism $f$ to the functor $f^{\ast}\circ y_{\cal C}$. The two correspondences are quasi-inverses to each other since, on the one hand, for any functor $A:{\cal C}\to {\cal E}$, $L_{A}\circ y_{\cal C}\cong A$ and, on the other hand, for any weak morphism $f:{\cal E}\to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, $f^{\ast}\cong L_{f^{\ast}\circ y_{\cal C}}$ since both functors preserve arbitrary colimits (as they have right adjoints) and their composites with the Yoneda embedding are isomorphic to the same functor (namely, $f^{\ast}\circ y_{\cal C}$).
nodes.statement_short: Quasi-inverse assignments via Yoneda

nodes.name: Restriction to $J$-continuous functors
nodes.statement: (ii) If $A$ is $J$-continuous then $R_{A}$ factors through the canonical inclusion ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$. Regarded as a functor ${\cal E}\to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$, it preserves arbitrary limits (since ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ is closed in $[{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ under arbitrary limits), so it has a left adjoint and hence defines a weak morphism of toposes $g:{\cal E}\to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ which, composed with the canonical geometric inclusion $i_{J}:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, gives the weak morphism induced by $A$; in particular, the inverse image $g^{\ast}:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$ of this morphism satisfies $g^{\ast}\circ a_{J}\cong L_{A}$. This also shows that the functor $A$ corresponding to $i_{J}\circ g$ is given by $g^{\ast}\circ l$; indeed, $A\cong L_{A}\circ y_{\cal C}\cong g^{\ast}\circ a_{J}\circ y_{\cal C}\cong g^{\ast}\circ l$. Conversely, given a weak morphism $f:{\cal E}\to [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ corresponding as in (i) to a functor $A:{\cal C}\to {\cal E}$ (so that $f^{\ast}\cong L_{A}$ and $f_{\ast}\cong R_{A}$), if $f$ factors through ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$ then $f_{\ast}$ (that is, $R_{A}$) factors through the direct image of the geometric inclusion ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)\hookrightarrow [{\cal C}^{\textup{op}}, {\bf Set }]$, that is, $A$ is $J$-continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction to $J$-continuous functors

nodes.name: List the four claims to prove
nodes.statement: We have to prove that: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item For any $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $A:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$, the geometric morphism $C_{A}$ it induces is essential. \item For any essential geometric morphism ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$, the functor $f_{!}\circ l$ is a $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$. \item Any essential geometric morphism $f:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$ is equal to $C_{f_{!}\circ l}$. \item Any $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $A:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$ satisfies $A\cong (C_{A})_{!}\circ l$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: List the four claims to prove
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Claim (i)
nodes.statement: \item For any $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $A:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$, the geometric morphism $C_{A}$ it induces is essential.
nodes.statement_short: Claim (i)
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Claim (ii)
nodes.statement: \item For any essential geometric morphism ${\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$, the functor $f_{!}\circ l$ is a $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim (ii)
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Claim (iii)
nodes.statement: \item Any essential geometric morphism $f:{\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J) \to {\cal E}$ is equal to $C_{f_{!}\circ l}$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim (iii)
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: Claim (iv)
nodes.statement: \item Any $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $A:({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$ satisfies $A\cong (C_{A})_{!}\circ l$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Claim (iv)
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $C_A$ is essential with $R_A$ as inverse image
nodes.statement: (i) By Proposition \ref{propweakmorphismequivalence}(ii), $A$ induces a pair of adjoint functors $L_{A} \dashv R_{A}$, where $R_{A}$ is the functor ${\cal E} \to {\bf Sh}({\cal C}, J)$ given by: $e\mapsto \textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(A(-), e)$. Now, $R_{A}$ corresponds to the inverse image of the geometric morphism $C_{A}$ induced by $A$ under the equivalence ${\cal E}\simeq {\bf Sh}({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$; indeed, by Theorem 4 at p. 412 of \cite{MM}, $C_{A}^{\ast}(P)\cong a_{J}(P\circ A^{\textup{op}})$ for any $P\in {\bf Sh}({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$, whence, by taking $P=\textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(-, e)$, $C_{A}^{\ast}(\textup{Hom}_{\cal E}(-, e))\cong R_{A}(e)$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: $C_A$ is essential with $R_A$ as inverse image
nodes.section: 4.3 Continuous comorphisms of sites and essential geometric morphisms

nodes.name: $f_!\circ l$ is continuous and has covering-lifting
nodes.statement: (ii) Any essential geometric morphism of sites induces an adjunction $(f_{!}\dashv f^{\ast})$; so, by Proposition \ref{propweakmorphismequivalence}(ii), the functor $f_{!}\circ l$ is $J$-continuous. It remains to prove that $f_{!}\circ l$ is a $J$-continuous comorphism of sites $({\cal C}, J) \to ({\cal E}, J^{\textup{can}}_{\cal E})$.
